## Predictive accuracy from one fit

Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO) asks how well a model predicts each
observation when that observation is left out of the fit. Summed over the
observations, this is the expected log predictive density,
$\mathrm{elpd}_{\mathrm{loo}}$, and it compares models on the scale of the
data, whatever their parameters.

Refitting once per observation is slow. `loo()` gets the answer from the one
fit, with no refits and no posterior draws: it expands each observation's
log-likelihood to second order around the posterior (Alhyari et al., 2026).
`waic()` gives the widely applicable information criterion from the same
expansion.

Both need the log-likelihood one observation at a time, which
`inla_vanilla()` never sees. So write the model in three pieces:

1. `loglik(theta, ...)`, the vector of log-likelihood terms, one per
   observation;
2. `logprior(theta)`, the log-prior, with any Jacobian;
3. `logpost(theta, ...)`, which is `sum(loglik(theta, ...)) +
   logprior(theta)`.

Fit with `logpost`, then pass `loglik` to `loo()` and `waic()`.

## Warp breaks

The `warpbreaks` data count the breaks in the warp yarn on 54 looms, by wool
(A or B) and tension (low, medium or high), with nine looms for each of the
six combinations. We model the counts on the log scale, with an interaction
between wool and tension.

```{r}
#| label: data
library(inlavanilla)

y <- warpbreaks$breaks
X <- model.matrix(~ wool * tension, data = warpbreaks)
colnames(X)[1] <- "intercept"
```

### A Poisson model

The log-likelihood terms, the log-prior and their sum:

```{r}
#| label: poisson
loglik_pois <- function(theta, X, y) {
  dpois(y, lambda = exp(drop(X %*% theta)), log = TRUE)
}
logprior_beta <- function(beta) {
  # N(0, 5^2) on the intercept and N(0, 2.5^2) on the effects
  sum(dnorm(beta, 0, c(5, rep(2.5, length(beta) - 1)), log = TRUE))
}
logpost_pois <- function(theta, X, y) {
  sum(loglik_pois(theta, X, y)) + logprior_beta(theta)
}

init_pois <- setNames(numeric(ncol(X)), colnames(X))
fit_pois <- inla_vanilla(logpost_pois, init_pois, X = X, y = y)
```

`loo()` takes the fit, `loglik`, and the same data:

```{r}
#| label: loo-poisson
loo_pois <- loo(fit_pois, loglik_pois, X = X, y = y)
loo_pois
```

`p_loo` is the effective number of parameters. Here it is about 21, for a
model with 6 parameters: a sign that the model is misspecified. The counts
vary much more than a Poisson distribution allows.

### A negative binomial model

The negative binomial adds a dispersion parameter $\phi$: the variance is
$\mu + \mu^2 / \phi$. On the unconstrained scale the parameter is
$\log \phi$, and the prior $\phi \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(2, 0.1)$ needs the
Jacobian of $\phi = e^{\log \phi}$, which is $\log \phi$ itself on the log
scale:

```{r}
#| label: negbin
loglik_nb <- function(theta, X, y) {
  beta <- theta[seq_len(ncol(X))]
  dnbinom(
    y,
    size = exp(theta[["log_phi"]]),
    mu = exp(drop(X %*% beta)),
    log = TRUE
  )
}
logprior_nb <- function(theta) {
  phi <- exp(theta[["log_phi"]])
  logprior_beta(theta[names(theta) != "log_phi"]) +
    dgamma(phi, shape = 2, rate = 0.1, log = TRUE) +
    theta[["log_phi"]] # the Jacobian
}
logpost_nb <- function(theta, X, y) {
  sum(loglik_nb(theta, X, y)) + logprior_nb(theta)
}

init_nb <- c(init_pois, log_phi = 2)
fit_nb <- inla_vanilla(logpost_nb, init_nb, X = X, y = y, silent = TRUE)
loo_nb <- loo(fit_nb, loglik_nb, X = X, y = y)
loo_nb
```

Now `p_loo` is close to the 7 parameters.

## Comparing the models

The difference in elpd between two models fitted to the same observations,
and its standard error, come from the paired differences of their pointwise
terms:

```{r}
#| label: diff
elpd_diff <- function(a, b) {
  d <- a$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - b$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]
  c(elpd_diff = sum(d), se = sqrt(length(d)) * sd(d))
}
elpd_diff(loo_nb, loo_pois)
```

The negative binomial predicts better, by about four standard errors. Does it
need the interaction? Fit the additive model with the same log-likelihood and
prior, on a smaller design matrix:

```{r}
#| label: additive
X_add <- model.matrix(~ wool + tension, data = warpbreaks)
colnames(X_add)[1] <- "intercept"
init_add <- c(setNames(numeric(ncol(X_add)), colnames(X_add)), log_phi = 2)

fit_add <- inla_vanilla(logpost_nb, init_add, X = X_add, y = y, silent = TRUE)
loo_add <- loo(fit_add, loglik_nb, X = X_add, y = y)
elpd_diff(loo_nb, loo_add)
```

The interaction model is ahead, but by less than one standard error: the data
cannot tell the two apart.

The results have the layout of the loo package's objects, so
`loo::loo_compare()` gives the same comparison as a table:

```{r}
#| label: loo-compare
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE)
loo::loo_compare(list(poisson = loo_pois, nb = loo_nb, nb_additive = loo_add))
```

`waic()` takes the same arguments. With no observation dominating the fit,
it is close to the LOO:

```{r}
#| label: waic
waic(fit_nb, loglik_nb, X = X, y = y)
```

## Checking against refitting

The brute-force LOO refits the model without each observation in turn and
averages that observation's likelihood over the refitted posterior:
$$
\log p(y_i \mid y_{-i}) = \log \int p(y_i \mid \vartheta) \,
p(\vartheta \mid y_{-i}) \, d\vartheta.
$$
Here the integral is an average over copula draws. The draws need only the
skew-normal marginals, so the refits skip the VB correction.

```{r}
#| label: refit
set.seed(1)
refit_elpd <- function(i) {
  fit_i <- inla_vanilla(
    logpost_nb,
    init_nb,
    X = X[-i, ],
    y = y[-i],
    vb = FALSE,
    silent = TRUE
  )
  ll <- sampling(
    fit_i,
    4000,
    fun = loglik_nb,
    X = X[i, , drop = FALSE],
    y = y[i]
  )
  max(ll) + log(mean(exp(ll - max(ll))))
}
time_refit <- system.time(
  elpd_refit <- vapply(seq_along(y), refit_elpd, numeric(1))
)
time_loo <- system.time(loo(fit_nb, loglik_nb, X = X, y = y))

c(refits = time_refit[["elapsed"]], loo = time_loo[["elapsed"]])
c(refits = sum(elpd_refit), loo = loo_nb$estimates["elpd_loo", "Estimate"])
```

```{r}
#| label: refit-plot
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of the pointwise elpd from loo() against the brute-force refits, one point per loom. The points lie on the identity line."
plot(
  elpd_refit,
  loo_nb$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"],
  xlab = "Refitting without each loom",
  ylab = "loo()",
  main = "Pointwise elpd",
  font.main = 1,
  pch = 21,
  bg = grDevices::adjustcolor("#C2410C", 0.5),
  col = "#C2410C",
  las = 1,
  bty = "n"
)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

The two agree loom by loom, to within
`r signif(max(abs(loo_nb$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"] - elpd_refit)), 1)` nats,
and their totals differ by
`r signif(abs(sum(loo_nb$pointwise[, "elpd_loo"]) - sum(elpd_refit)), 1)`, a
tenth of the standard error. `loo()` took a fraction of the time of the 54
refits.

## Leaving out what?

`loglik` decides the unit that is left out. One term per observation leaves
out one observation at a time. For grouped data, sum each group's terms, so
that `loglik` returns one term per group: `loo()` then leaves out a whole
group at a time, and estimates how well the model predicts a new group
(leave-one-cluster-out; Alhyari et al., 2026). Either way the units must be
conditionally independent given the parameters, so that the log-likelihood is
the sum of the terms.

## Influential observations

Each unit's `k`, in `pointwise[, "k"]`, is the largest share of the posterior
precision it carries in any direction of the parameter space. A value close to
1 means that the unit alone pins down some combination of the parameters.
At $k \ge 1$ the rest of the data and the prior cannot identify that
combination without it, the second-order term does not exist, and `loo()`
falls back to the first-order expansion for every unit, with a warning. Here
no loom comes close:

```{r}
#| label: leverage
summary(loo_nb$pointwise[, "k"])
```
